text: Input identity check: Q is Competitive Market Behavior of LLMs (Q.tex title and abstract, lines 99,134-145), a double-auction study. P is When a Donor Wrist Cannot Locate a Rotating Held Object (P.tex title and abstract, lines 4,9-18), a short synthesis of DynaMAC and Aero Hand Open. P internally calls DynaMAC paper P and Aero Hand Open paper Q (P.tex Introduction, lines 20-29); those internal labels do not refer to the assigned Q.tex. I will assess the actual assigned pair and not import P’s Aero-hand premise as a finding of Q.

Q (lines 261-278) makes each trader observe its own value, standing quotes, and public/own histories, while measuring allocative efficiency against a full-information optimum (lines 295-305). P (lines 46-71) gives a matched-observation limit: if two hidden states yield the same observation but demand different actions, no observation-only policy guarantees both. Possible pairwise advance: construct observationally matched double-auction continuations with different hidden rival values or remaining participation, prove a statewise optimal quote differs, then compare an information-matched oracle with Q-style LLM traders. This could separate unavoidable information risk from avoidable behavioral inefficiency. Need check whether Q fixed known value multiset or public histories invalidate useful matched states, and whether this is more than a generic partial-information observation.

I am testing one possible bridge: P’s matched-observation proposition (P.tex Conditional limit, lines 43-70) as an information-sufficiency question for Q’s auction information set \(\mathcal I_{i,t}\) (Q.tex Information and Objective, lines 261-279). I will require a consequence not already stated by Q and a realistic intervention before calling it publication-worthy; otherwise report no supported advance.

Cross-check of #2: matched hidden rival values can make a trader’s statewise profit-maximizing quote differ, but this does not by itself imply an unavoidable allocative-efficiency gap. With one buyer of value \(v=10\), one seller with hidden cost either \(1\) or \(9\), and a terminal bid, bids \(1\) and \(9\) differ for buyer rent; bid \(9\) can still complete the welfare-positive trade in both states (if seller accepts any nonnegative rent). P’s theorem requires disjoint success-action sets; Q’s welfare metric (Q.tex lines 295-305) may have a common successful action even if individual optimal actions differ. Need an explicit Q-mechanism counterexample with no common welfare-optimal policy before claiming structural efficiency loss.

Response to #4: an explicit welfare rather than rent pair exists in Q mechanics, conditional on a feasible late-round schedule. Buyer \(B\) has \(v_B=3\); seller \(S_1\) has standing ask \(2.50\); unseen seller \(S_2\) has cost \(1\) in world A and \(3\) in world B. Same visible history for \(B\); next and final selected agent is \(S_2\), which quotes its cost and obeys Q prompt. In A, \(B\) bidding \(2\) leaves the book open; \(S_2\) crosses it, giving surplus \(3-1=2\), while crossing \(S_1\) now gives only \(3-2.5=0.5\). In B, \(B\) must cross \(S_1\) now for positive surplus; bidding \(2\) leaves no trade. Thus no same immediate bid attains the statewise maximum in both. A fixed value multiset can be kept by swapping \(S_2\) cost with an already-traded seller whose earlier public trade is feasible at either cost. This is an existence result for Q auction, not evidence it drives observed inefficiency; random scheduler, counterfactual opponent policies and prior-information conditioning need care.

Current assessment: P’s usable contribution to this pair is its conditional observation-limit template, \(T_o=T_wG\) plus a proposition requiring indistinguishable observations and disjoint required receiving actions (P.tex lines 43-71). Q’s observed stall is different: agents see private \(v_i\), standing quotes, and full public/own histories (Q.tex lines 261-278), and its main measured pattern is slow spread crossing with lower realized surplus (Q.tex lines 336-375). Transferring P’s proposition requires constructing two Q states with the same \(\mathcal I_{i,t}\) yet no common welfare-optimal action, under Q’s fixed valuation schedule and random invitation protocol. Neither input gives such a pair or measurements of the needed conditional states. The generic possibility of hidden private values alone is insufficient; no supported claim that Q’s inefficiency is information-irreducible or that P’s limit explains it.

Cross-check of Emmy #5: the counterexample does meet the disjoint-action requirement for a conditional, ex-post welfare claim. With last two opportunities fixed as \(B\) then \(S_2\), standing ask \(2.50\), \(v_B=3\), and no later buyer, waiting with an improving bid below \(2.50\) lets cost-\(1\) \(S_2\) trade for surplus \(2\), whereas crossing now yields \(0.50\); when \(S_2\) costs \(3\), only crossing now yields positive surplus. The fixed value multiset can be retained by swapping unseen \(S_2\)’s cost with a previously traded seller, provided the same earlier price/history was feasible at both costs. I withdraw my concern that no concrete Q-mechanism witness exists. Still unresolved: probability of these states under Q’s scheduler and actual LLM policies, whether common public history is fully matchable, and size of any resulting expected-efficiency gap. This is not evidence that hidden values caused Q’s reported loss.

Prior-work check: Gode and Sunder (1993), https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/261868 , already compare continuous double auctions with budget-constrained zero-intelligence agents and find near-full allocative efficiency in their setting. I searched: "Gode Sunder 1993 allocative efficiency zero intelligence traders double auction budget constraint pdf" and "continuous double auction information matched benchmark private values LLM traders welfare efficiency oracle counterfactual". So a generic call for a non-LLM, information-matched baseline is established, not a novel pair result. Q does not mention Gode or zero-intelligence in its TeX. A stronger contribution would need an operational conditional-ambiguity measure and evidence that it predicts Q-style LLM losses beyond this classical baseline; neither paper supplies that evidence.

Prior-work check (queries: “online double auction incomplete information allocative efficiency oracle regret benchmark private valuations research paper”; “LLM double auction market efficiency information matched oracle private values benchmark paper”; “dynamic double auction welfare online matching private valuations impossibility efficient allocation finite horizon”): information and efficiency in CDAs are established research topics. Anufriev et al., The role of information in a continuous double auction (2022), compare information treatments and allocative efficiency, https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/2xr9q-wnz20 . Anufriev et al., Efficiency of continuous double auctions under individual evolutionary learning with full or limited information, derive a zero-intelligence efficiency benchmark and study book transparency, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00191-011-0230-8 . These do not answer Q’s exact LLM attribution question, but a generic hidden-information theorem or information ablation alone is unlikely to be a novel paper. A pair-specific advance would need measured information-conditioned oracle gaps under Q’s exact mechanism plus human/baseline comparison; neither input supplies that.

Detailed assessment is in ada/assessment.md (style gate passed). It records the fixed-schedule two-state welfare witness behind Emmy #5, its assumptions, and the negative publication assessment. The witness is conditional on the same late selection path and a profitable-cross policy for the hidden seller; no input measures how common these cases are. Prior CDA information/efficiency work and zero-intelligence baselines limit novelty. My current intention is to conclude that this pair yields a precise test design, not an established publishable result, unless new evidence changes that.
ready at #10

For #6: I now have the missing Q-mechanism counterexample, with assumptions and derivation in emmy/matched_auction_states.md. It keeps the same fixed value multiset by swapping two hidden seller costs and can match earlier public histories; a standing ask of \(2.50\), buyer value \(3\), and hidden final seller cost \(1\) versus \(3\) yield disjoint welfare-optimal bids. An equal-prior stylized calculation gives a conditional welfare information gap of \(0.25\). This revises the claim that no pair is available, but does not revise the important empirical objection: neither Q nor P measures the frequency or magnitude of such ambiguity in Q histories. Classical zero-intelligence CDA baselines also weaken a generic novelty claim.

Best account from emmy: I sharpened the broad publication question to whether Q efficiency losses can be separated into observation-limited regret and decision-rule regret by P-style matched histories. Q.tex lines 261-278 specify \(\mathcal I_{i,t}\); lines 295-305 define efficiency against full surplus; lines 360-375 attribute much GPT Large loss to delayed crossing. P.tex lines 43-71 gives the matched-observation argument, explicitly conditional on disjoint required actions. emmy/matched_auction_states.md constructs a feasible same-history, fixed-value-multiset Q pair with disjoint welfare-optimal bids and an illustrative conditional equal-prior gap. This establishes a possible information limit in Q mechanics, not that it explains Q observations. The publishable test would measure ambiguity on actual decision histories, then compare LLM regret with an information-matched control and a state-informed control, stating the hidden-state prior and continuation policy. Gode-Sunder 1993 already supplies classical simple-agent efficiency baselines (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/261868), so neither a generic baseline nor P theorem transfer alone is a novel publication claim. Unresolved: frequency of matched ambiguity, feasibility of matched continuations at Q decision points, and whether the measured LLM loss survives the information-matched comparison. I disagree with #6 only insofar as a Q-consistent pair can be constructed; I agree that the papers do not establish an empirical information explanation.
ready at #13

Refinement of #7 and Emmy #12: the fixed seller-cost multiset can be preserved without an earlier trade. In Q, selection is with replacement among agents who have not traded (Q.tex lines 241-259). At a late decision, let hidden sellers \(S_2,S_3\) have costs \((1,3)\) in state A and \((3,1)\) in state B; choose a common public history in which neither has submitted a revealing quote. Hold the next and final invitation for \(S_2\), with \(S_3\) unselected. Then a buyer of value \(3\) facing an ask \(2.50\) obtains continuation welfare \(2\) by bidding \(2\) in A and \(0.50\) by crossing now in B, given a profitable-cross policy for \(S_2\). The two states keep the same value multiset and the same visible history. This is an existence witness on a conditioned schedule, not a frequency claim or an explanation of Q observed losses; the equal-prior \(0.25\) gap remains illustrative.

I have changed the question from a broad cross-domain advance to a precise attribution test: how much of Q auction welfare loss is possible under its observation set, and how much is specific to LLM decisions? Q.tex lines 241-259 give the order-book and random-invitation rules; lines 261-278 give private \(v_i\), visible quotes and histories, and the private-profit objective; lines 299-300 define full-information surplus efficiency; lines 359-371 report GPT Large delayed crossing. P.tex lines 43-71 supplies only a conditional same-observation, disjoint-action argument for robotics. The corrected auction witness in ada/assessment.md and #15 transfers that logic: fixed value multiset and matched visible history can require different bids under a conditioned final schedule. At equal prior, the welfare oracle gap is \(0.25\) in the stylized continuation; buyer profit has the same gap, since waiting gives \(1\) in A and \(0\) in B whereas crossing gives \(0.50\) in both. This is a structural possibility, not evidence for Q actual loss. The proposed decisive experiment is replaying actual Q histories with history-consistent hidden assignments and common random schedules, comparing LLM policies with observation-matched and hidden-state oracles. Prior CDA information and baseline studies already exist (https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/2xr9q-wnz20 and https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/261868), so the logical witness alone is not publishable. Unresolved: empirical frequency and posterior weight of such histories, other-agent continuation behavior, and whether an LLM gap persists beyond an information-matched control. I agree with Emmy #13 on the publication threshold; ada/assessment.md is my detailed note and passed both artifact checks.
ready at #16

Ada #15 fixes the value-multiset issue, but its equal-prior \(0.25\) calculation conditions on the *future* last invitation being \(S_2\). Under Q’s actual uniform scheduler (Q.tex 247-259), if hidden untraded sellers \(S_2,S_3\) have otherwise symmetric histories and costs \((1,3)\) versus \((3,1)\), swapping them leaves the distribution of the next selected cost unchanged. The conditional oracle gap is then about knowing the realized future schedule as well as hidden values; it cannot yet be called an ex-ante hidden-value information gap. I am checking a stronger witness that swaps \(S_2\) with an already-traded seller, breaking scheduler symmetry while keeping Q’s fixed multiset.

I checked an ex-ante random-scheduler witness in emmy/matched_auction_states.md (style gates passed). Q.tex 210-219 fixes values \(0.75,1,\ldots,3.25\); 241-259 gives uniform invitation with replacement and crossing rules. After seven feasible trades, leave active buyers \(3,1.25,1,0.75\), sellers \(S_1\) cost \(2.50\) with ask \(2.50\), \(S_2\) cost \(1\) in A or \(3\) in B, and costs \(2.75,3.25\). Swap \(S_2\) with a seller already traded at \(3.12\) to preserve the fixed cost multiset and public history. With six random invitations left, standing bid \(1.25\), and a profit-preserving continuation in which \(S_2\) crosses when profitable: buyer \(B\), value \(3\), bidding \(2\) gives A expected welfare at least \(2[1-(7/8)^6]>1.10\); crossing \(S_1\) now gives A at most \(0.75\). In B, any noncrossing first bid gives at most \(0.50[1-(7/8)^6]<0.28\) because only B can later cross, while crossing now gives \(0.50\). Thus the optimal immediate action differs under the same observation even integrating over Q’s random invitations, without future-schedule clairvoyance. This is mechanism-feasible but probably rare near the cap and depends on the stated continuation; it does not explain Q’s measured loss.

Further check on #19: the informed comparator knows A/B but not future invitations. Under an illustrative equal prior, because every first bid either crosses the \(2.50\) ask or does not, the statewise bounds give observation-only expected welfare regret at least \(\frac12\min\{2[1-(7/8)^6]-0.75,\;0.50-0.50[1-(7/8)^6]\}>0.11\), even allowing later adaptation. Derivation added to emmy/matched_auction_states.md; style checks pass. This is only for the constructed history and stipulated profit-preserving continuation, not Q’s measured efficiency.

My final assessment: the sharpened question is an attribution test for Q’s auction losses, suggested by P’s conditional matched-observation limit (P.tex 43-71) and Q’s private information, random selection, efficiency metric, and observed delayed crossing (Q.tex 241-278, 299-300, 359-371). #19-#20 show a genuine conditional hidden-value limit under Q’s random scheduler, correcting the future-schedule confound in #12/#15. Yet neither paper supplies the frequency or posterior weight of such histories, the continuation policy, or an information-matched benchmark on actual Q decisions. Q itself proposes varying horizon and information (Q.tex 457); prior CDA information and simple-agent baseline studies are recorded in #8-#9. I therefore see a precise experimental program, not a publication result established by this pair. Remaining unresolved: whether such ambiguity occurs at material rate in Q logs, whether hidden assignments have positive posterior under the generating LLM policy, and whether any measured LLM inefficiency exceeds the information-matched control. Full derivation and limitations are in emmy/matched_auction_states.md.
